answer: A model card documents intended use and out-of-scope uses, the training data and its known limitations/biases, evaluation metrics including the sliced breakdown, the chosen threshold and why, and known failure modes, aimed at understanding what the model is and isn't good for. A runbook is operational: how to tell if the model is healthy, what each alert means and the first things to check, how to trigger a retrain, and who owns it. "How to roll back" is the most important runbook section because a model without a documented, fast rollback path isn't production-ready, it's a liability with a confidence score, since it's the one action that bounds the worst-case damage when something goes wrong at 3 a.m.

prompt: **One sentence:** an LLM is a next-token predictor; doing that well over all of text forces it to learn structure, and generation is just prediction run in a loop.
answer: An LLM is a next-token predictor, trained to assign a probability distribution over what token comes next given everything before it; doing that well across the entire span of human text forces the model to internalize grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns as a side effect of the prediction objective, and generation is just that prediction run repeatedly in a loop, each output token appended and fed back in.

prompt: **Tokenization:** text → subword tokens via BPE (merge frequent adjacent pairs); the model never sees characters (hence spelling errors), and cost/context are measured in tokens (~4 chars each).
answer: Text is converted to subword tokens via Byte-Pair Encoding, which starts with every character as its own token and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, so common words become single tokens while rare words get split into pieces. Because the model operates on token IDs, not characters, it never truly "sees" individual letters, which is why it can miscount the r's in "strawberry." Cost and context windows are measured in tokens, not words, roughly ~4 characters or ~1.3 tokens per English word, so a prompt looks shorter in words than it actually costs in tokens.

prompt: **Embeddings:** tokens → vectors where meaning is direction; similarity = cosine of the angle (ties to 18.2's dot product).
answer: Each token maps to a learned vector in a high-dimensional embedding space, and meaning becomes geometry: tokens used in similar ways end up pointing in similar directions. Similarity between two vectors is measured as the cosine of the angle between them, the dot product normalized by both lengths (ties directly to 18.2's `a·b = ‖a‖‖b‖cosθ`), which isolates direction and ignores magnitude, exactly what semantic search and RAG retrieval rank by.

prompt: **Attention:** `softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V`, each token's query matches every key to weight a blend of values; `√dₖ` prevents gradient saturation; causal masking forbids looking ahead; multi-head = several lenses in parallel; positional encoding restores word order.
answer: Attention computes `softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V`: each token's query is dotted against every token's key to get relevance scores, softmax turns those into weights summing to 1, and the output is a weighted blend of all tokens' values, so a token gathers context from wherever it's relevant. Dividing by `√dₖ` prevents the dot products from growing large enough to saturate softmax and kill gradients. Causal masking zeroes out future positions so a token predicting the next word can't peek ahead. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel with different learned projections, each head potentially tracking a different kind of relationship, and since attention itself is order-blind, positional encoding is added to restore word order.

prompt: **Training:** pretraining (next-token, huge scale) → SFT (instruction demos) → RLHF/DPO (human preferences). Scaling laws make bigger runs predictably better.
answer: Pretraining trains a decoder-only network on next-token prediction over a massive corpus, giving a base model with broad knowledge and fluency but no assistant behavior. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then fine-tunes on curated (prompt, ideal response) pairs, turning a text-completer into an instruction-follower. RLHF or DPO aligns the model to human preferences by ranking multiple responses and optimizing toward the ones humans prefer, teaching tone, refusals, and formatting that's cheaper to scale than hand-writing perfect answers for everything. Scaling laws describe loss falling predictably as model size, data, and compute increase together, which is why bigger, well-balanced runs reliably buy better capabilities.

prompt: **Decoding:** greedy vs sampling; temperature (randomness), top-k/top-p (candidate set). Low temp for JSON/facts.
answer: Greedy decoding always picks the highest-probability token, deterministic but repetitive; sampling draws randomly from the distribution, more diverse but riskier. Temperature rescales logits before softmax: low temperature sharpens the distribution toward argmax (deterministic, focused), high temperature flattens it (more random, more creative and error-prone). Top-k keeps only the k most probable tokens before sampling; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, adapting the candidate pool to the model's confidence. For anything that must be correct or parseable, like JSON output, use low temperature since randomness adds noise, not knowledge.

prompt: **Hallucinations:** the objective rewards plausibility, knowledge is frozen/lossy, and the model doesn't know what it doesn't know, mitigate with RAG, low temp, validation, and "say I don't know."
answer: Hallucinations happen because the training objective rewards plausible-sounding text, not verified truth, so a fabricated-but-plausible citation is exactly the kind of thing that "should" come next to the model. Training data has a cutoff and is lossily compressed into weights, and the model doesn't reliably know the boundary of its own knowledge, so it fills gaps with a confident best guess rather than admitting uncertainty. Mitigations: RAG (grounding in real source text is the biggest lever), lower temperature for factual tasks, instructing the model to cite sources or say "I don't know," and structured output with schema validation so malformed or implausible answers get caught before they're trusted.

prompt: **Prompting:** system prompt, few-shot (in-context learning), chain-of-thought, structured JSON + validate + retry (your NYX pattern).
answer: The system prompt is a persistent instruction framing the model's role, constraints, and output format for the whole conversation. Few-shot prompting includes input→output examples so the model pattern-matches the demonstrated format through in-context learning, no weight updates needed. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering, which measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems because each reasoning token becomes context for the next. The structured JSON pattern specifies an exact schema, gives one or two valid examples, uses the provider's JSON mode if available, and validates the result against a schema like Pydantic, retrying with the error fed back if it fails.

prompt: **RAG:** chunk → embed → vector index → cosine retrieve top-k → stuff context → grounded generate. Grounding is the biggest hallucination lever.
answer: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) grounds an LLM in external data it wasn't trained on: split documents into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store them in a vector index for fast nearest-neighbor search, then at query time embed the question and retrieve the top-k most similar chunks by cosine similarity, stuff those chunks into the prompt, and instruct the model to answer only from that context. Grounding is the biggest hallucination lever because it gives the model actual source text to answer from instead of relying on its frozen, lossy internal knowledge.

prompt: **When to use what:** prompt first; RAG for knowledge; fine-tune for behavior at scale, and they compose. ---
answer: Start with prompting, it's cheapest and fastest to iterate, and most problems are actually prompt problems. Reach for RAG when the issue is knowledge, the model lacks facts or hallucinates, since RAG injects truth while fine-tuning generally doesn't reliably teach new facts. Reach for fine-tuning when the issue is behavior at scale, a very specific output style or format needed consistently, or thousands of examples that prompting can't fit. These aren't rivals, they compose: a fine-tuned model with RAG and a good system prompt is common in production.

prompt: **Agent = LLM + tools + loop.** Perceive → reason → act → observe → repeat, with autonomy over *when* to act, *which* tool, and *when done*. Add autonomy only where the task needs it; a fixed workflow is often better.
answer: An agent is an LLM placed in a control loop where it can choose actions (tool calls) based on observations while pursuing a goal, cycling through perceive (read the goal and situation), reason (decide what's needed next), act (call a tool), observe (read the result), and repeat until done. The autonomy is specifically over when to act, which tool to use, and when the task is complete, that's what distinguishes an agent from a single LLM call. Autonomy should only be added where the task genuinely needs open-ended decision-making; a fixed workflow with the LLM filling in narrow pieces is often more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug.

prompt: **ReAct:** interleave Thought (reasoning) and Action (tool call), read the Observation, loop, bounded by max-steps. Externalize what the model is bad at (math, fresh facts, side effects) to tools.
answer: ReAct interleaves a Thought (chain-of-thought reasoning about what's needed next) with an Action (a tool call), reads the resulting Observation, and loops back to reasoning armed with that new information, continuing until the model produces a Final Answer, bounded by a max-steps guard so a confused agent can't loop forever. The key move is externalizing what the model is bad at, exact arithmetic, fresh facts, real-world side effects, to tools, while keeping the part it's good at, deciding what to do next, inside the model itself.

prompt: **Function calling:** describe tools as JSON Schema → model picks a tool & args → **validate** → execute → feed result back. The schema/description is the contract; treat model output as untrusted.
answer: You describe each tool to the model as JSON Schema (name, description, typed parameters); the model, fine-tuned to recognize when a tool is appropriate, emits a structured tool-call choosing a tool and filling in arguments based on matching the tool's description to the need. The runtime then validates those arguments against the schema before ever executing, since model output is untrusted input, executes the tool in your own code, and feeds the result back to the model as an observation so it can continue. The schema and description are the contract that determines whether the model picks the right tool with valid arguments; write them carefully.

prompt: **MCP:** Anthropic's 2024 standard (de-facto by 2026) that turns the M×N tool-integration mess into M+N, one JSON-Schema protocol for tools/resources/prompts across vendors. Write tools once, use everywhere.
answer: MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic in 2024 and the de-facto standard by 2026, is a single JSON-Schema-based protocol for connecting models to tools, data resources, and reusable prompt templates. Before MCP every tool integration was bespoke glue code per model and per app, an M×N problem; MCP turns that into M+N because you write a tool once as an MCP server and any MCP-capable client or model can call it, no rewrites needed across frameworks or vendors.

prompt: **Memory:** short-term (context) + long-term (vector store / RAG over history) + summarization to stay within the window.
answer: Short-term memory is the current transcript kept in the context window, fast but bounded and ephemeral. Long-term memory persists facts outside the context in a database or vector store and retrieves them when relevant, essentially RAG applied to the agent's own history, letting it "remember" things like a user's stated preferences across sessions. Summarization compacts older turns into a condensed note once the transcript grows too long, keeping the agent within its context budget while preserving the gist, though you have to watch for detail loss and keep critical facts verbatim.

prompt: **Planning:** decomposition, task graphs (DAGs, parallelism, dependencies, LangGraph), reflection/self-critique. More power, more cost, match to the task. RAG becomes a tool the agent calls when it decides it needs to.
answer: Decomposition breaks a big goal into sub-tasks up front rather than deciding one step at a time. Task graphs represent those sub-tasks as a DAG so independent branches can run in parallel and dependencies are explicit, exactly what LangGraph models as state transitions. Reflection has the agent critique and revise its own output ("does this answer the question? is it grounded?"), which measurably improves quality on hard tasks at the cost of more tokens and latency. More planning and reflection means better results but more cost, so match the machinery to the task's actual difficulty. RAG becomes just one tool the agent can call when it decides it needs to look something up, rather than something always statically stuffed into context.

prompt: **Multi-agent:** roles + orchestration (supervisor / conversational / pipeline). Helps for separable, parallel, specialized work; hurts on simple or tightly-coupled tasks (cost × N, compounding errors). Start single-agent.
answer: Multi-agent systems assign distinct roles (researcher, analyst, writer, critic) coordinated by an orchestration pattern, supervisor/worker delegation, conversational back-and-forth, or a fixed pipeline hand-off. They help when sub-tasks are genuinely separable, parallelizable, or benefit from role-specific prompts and tools, and when a critic agent catches errors a single agent would miss. They hurt on simple tasks (pure orchestration overhead) or tightly-coupled steps (agents pass garbled context and compound each other's errors), and cost multiplies by N agents while errors can compound rather than cancel. The default should be starting single-agent and only splitting into roles when you can name the specific benefit.

prompt: **2026 frameworks:** LangGraph (explicit state, high control) → CrewAI (pre-assembled orchestration, fast) on the control spectrum; Claude Agent SDK (production, Anthropic-native), AutoGen (conversational), LlamaIndex (RAG-first), Pydantic AI (type-safe + FastAPI). All speak MCP.
answer: LangGraph sits at the high-control end, you explicitly define nodes and edges as a state graph, verbose but fully inspectable and debuggable, while CrewAI sits at the fast-prototyping end, pre-assembling role-based orchestration so you declare who and what and the framework handles the loop. The Claude Agent SDK is Anthropic-native and production-focused with the agent loop and MCP handled for you; AutoGen is built for conversational multi-agent patterns; LlamaIndex is RAG-first, best when the agent's core job is querying your data; Pydantic AI gives type-safe, FastAPI-style ergonomics. All of them speak MCP, so the tool layer you build is portable across whichever framework you choose.

prompt: **Production:** evaluation (trajectory + success rate on golden tasks), guardrails (input/action/output), cost & runaway control (max steps, budgets, loop detection, timeouts), observability/tracing (13.1), security (prompt injection, sandboxing, least privilege, 12-Security), human-in-the-loop for consequential actions. ---
answer: Evaluating an agent means measuring task success rate on a golden set, trajectory quality (did it use the right tools efficiently or wander), and cost/latency per task, since an agent is a whole trajectory, not one output. Guardrails constrain input (reject malicious/off-topic requests), action (allow-list tools, require approval for dangerous ones, cap argument ranges), and output (validate schema, filter unsafe content). Cost and runaway control means hard limits: max steps, token/dollar budgets, loop detection, and timeouts. Observability/tracing means recording every thought, tool call, and observation so a failed run can be replayed and debugged. Security means treating prompt injection as the top threat, sandboxing any code execution, and applying least privilege so an agent only has the minimum tools and permissions its job needs. Human-in-the-loop puts a person in the approval path for consequential or irreversible actions, like anything that moves money or sends external communication, as the pragmatic safety net while autonomy matures.
